  Maladaptive Strategies: Worst Case Rehearsal: mentally rehearse worst case scenarios to feel prepared, Avoid Anniversaries: Dates or anniversaries connected to the event, Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost
  Threat: Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again, Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively

Vignette:
# Rajesh

Rajesh was forty-two when his father died, though he still thinks of himself as thirty-nine—the age he was before everything changed. His father, Vikram, had complained of chest tightness one Thursday morning in Mumbai while Rajesh was in his studio in Portland, Oregon, reviewing fabric swatches for a high-end residential project. By the time Rajesh's mother called with the news, Vikram had already collapsed in the kitchen. He was gone before the ambulance arrived. The unexpectedness of it—the fact that his father had seemed fine just weeks earlier when they'd video-called, that there had been no warning, no chance to say anything—had carved something out of Rajesh that he still could not name.

The first year after his father's death, Rajesh had thrown himself into work with an intensity that impressed his colleagues and exhausted his wife, Priya. He redesigned three commercial spaces and two private homes, each project demanding his full attention in a way that felt necessary, protective. But as the anniversary of his father's death approached—November 14th—something shifted. Rajesh found himself unable to concentrate on a client meeting. His hands had begun to shake slightly as the date drew closer, and he'd started mentally rehearsing what would happen if Priya were to die next, if his mother's health would fail, if he would be utterly alone. These rehearsals felt important, urgent, as though by imagining the worst he might somehow prepare himself to survive it. He would lie awake at three in the morning constructing elaborate scenarios: a car accident on the drive to work, a sudden illness, a fall down the stairs. Each imagined catastrophe felt like a kind of armor, a way to inoculate himself against further loss.

By the second year, Rajesh had begun to avoid November entirely. He took vacation days when he could, kept his calendar deliberately light, and found reasons not to be home if Priya suggested plans. When his colleague Deepak mentioned that his mother had passed away and invited the team to the memorial service, Rajesh felt his throat tighten and his chest grow hot. He made an excuse about a client deadline and did not attend. The thought of being in a room where grief was being openly acknowledged, where people spoke about loss and remembered the dead, felt unbearable. He could not explain this to Priya without acknowledging that he was still undone by what had happened, and admitting that felt like weakness.

The avoidance had consequences he had not anticipated. Clients began to notice that Rajesh was unavailable in November and December. One important project had been reassigned to a junior designer because Rajesh could not commit to a timeline that spanned the anniversary. His relationship with Priya had grown strained; she had wanted to mark the anniversary together, to light a candle or call his mother, but Rajesh had insisted on working late those evenings. When she persisted, he had snapped at her with a harshness that shocked them both—his voice rising, his words cutting in ways he did not recognize in himself.

The flashbacks had begun without warning. He might be sitting in a client's living room, discussing paint colors, when suddenly he would feel the phone call happening again—the tremor in his mother's voice, the moment when he understood that his father was not coming back. His body would react first: his heart would race, his palms would sweat, and only then would his mind catch up to the fact that he was safe in Portland, not in Mumbai, that this was memory, not present danger. He had learned to excuse himself, to step into a bathroom or hallway, to breathe until the sensation passed. But the irritability was harder to hide. Small frustrations—a traffic delay, a contractor's miscommunication, Priya asking him a routine question about his day—would trigger an anger that felt disproportionate and uncontrollable. He would feel it rising in his chest before he could think, his voice sharpening, his words becoming weapons.

Three years after his father's death, Rajesh finally admitted to Priya that he needed help. The anniversary was approaching again, and he could not bear the thought of another year of this—the dread, the avoidance, the sudden rages that left him ashamed and isolated. He had come to believe that if he allowed himself to grieve, if he acknowledged the loss directly rather than trying to outrun it, he would somehow fall apart completely. But he was already falling apart, just more slowly, in ways that were damaging his marriage and his career. Priya had gently suggested that talking to someone might help him find a way forward that did not require him to disappear every autumn. Rajesh was terrified of what might emerge if he stopped running, but he was more afraid of losing what remained.
